title: Wings in twos and threes
hook: He made the angels messengers with wings, two, three and four (35:1)
carry: he adds to creation as he wills

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sheba, the people who let thanks run dry, and your line was gratitude keeps the garden. Which gift did you thank out loud? Today ends the week, and opens a new surah. Day five hundred forty-six.

Ask a child to draw an angel, and you'll get two wings, every time. White, feathered, one on each side, like a bird's. It's the picture from a thousand paintings and greeting cards. Surah thirty-five opens with angels too, and in its very first verse it breaks that picture open. Not two wings. Two, or three, or four. And then a line that suggests the count doesn't stop there. The surah is called Fatir, the Originator, the One who splits creation open from nothing, and it starts by refusing to let us think we've seen it all.

Verse one praises Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. Then, Pickthall: "Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will." Notice the word messengers. In the Qur'an, angels aren't decoration. They carry things: revelation, mercy, sometimes warning. And their wings come in numbers we aren't used to. The Arabic says mathna, wa thulath, wa ruba', in twos, and threes, and fours. Then the open door: yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha', He adds to creation whatever He wills. Many commentators read that as a hint that four isn't a limit. And a hadith gives one example. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form with six hundred wings. Six hundred. The verse and the hadith aren't giving an anatomy lesson. Muslims believe angels are real, but unseen, made of light, and that what we know of them comes only from revelation. The point is humility about our pictures. Whatever you imagine, creation is larger, and still being added to. That fits this week, actually. We met the Khadijah, Umm Salamah, and a blessing that starts with Allah and the angels before it reaches us. Mountains singing with Dawud. A termite that knew what the jinn didn't. A dam that broke when thanks ran dry. Again and again, the world in these surahs is bigger and stranger than the picture we walked in with.
screen: `HE ADDS TO CREATION AS HE WILLS.`

segments.voice: The practice: watch a bird fly. If you can, step to a window or outside and find one. Watch how the wings move, how often, how the bird turns. If no bird is near, picture the last one you saw. Notice how little you'd guessed about wings before you really looked. Then close your eyes and sit with the line, He adds to creation as He wills, and let it widen whatever picture you're holding. The bell holds the time.
Mathna, the word for 'in twos,' opening Surah Fatir's list of the angels' wings: in twos, and threes, and fours. Today's word.
Your line: he adds to creation as he wills. Today, when you think you've seen everything a place, a person or a day has to offer, look once more. Day five hundred forty-six, and the end of the week.

howItsDone: Belief in angels is one of the six articles of faith in Islam; Muslims understand them as unseen beings made of light who carry out Allah's commands, known only through the Qur'an and hadith.

original.note: Arabic: in twos, and threes, and fours, the angels' wings in 35:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: angels have two feathered wings.
what it means: angels are messengers with two, three or four wings, in a creation Allah keeps adding to.
what a scholar hears: the forms mathna, thulath, ruba' are distributive numbers; yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha' is read by many as open-ended, and Bukhari records Jibril's six hundred wings.
